fields.Text: Core functional requirements of a Twitter-like system include: {{c1::users can post tweets (text, optionally media)}}, {{c2::users can follow other users}}, and {{c3::users can view a timeline/feed of tweets from people they follow}}.

Non-functional requirements for Twitter-scale systems include: {{c1::high availability}}, {{c2::low read latency for feed generation}}, and {{c3::eventual consistency is acceptable (a slightly stale feed is fine)}}.

The high-level architecture of a Twitter-like system typically includes: {{c1::a tweet/write service}}, {{c2::a fanout/timeline-generation service}}, {{c3::a cache (e.g. Redis) storing precomputed timelines}}, and {{c4::a message queue between the write and fanout services}}.

Scaling bottlenecks and fixes for a Twitter-like feed system: {{c1::the tweets table growing huge}} is fixed by {{c2::sharding by user_id or tweet_id}}; {{c3::fanout write amplification for celebrities}} is fixed by {{c4::the hybrid push/pull model}}.

fields.Front: Should a Twitter-like system support near real-time delivery of new tweets to followers' feeds?
fields.Back: Yes — near real-time feed updates are expected as a functional requirement, typically within a few seconds of posting.

fields.Front: Why does a Twitter-like system favor availability and eventual consistency over strong consistency?
fields.Back: Feeds are read-heavy and users tolerate a few seconds of staleness in seeing new tweets, but not downtime — so the system is designed AP under CAP, using eventual consistency for feed propagation.

fields.Front: If a system has 200M daily active users posting 2 tweets/day on average, what is the approximate tweet-write QPS?
If each user checks their timeline 5 times/day and there are 200M DAU, what is the approximate read QPS for timeline requests?
Why is the read:write ratio for a social feed system typically very high (e.g. 100:1 or more)?
fields.Back: Far more users scroll/read feeds than post content, so read traffic (timeline fetches) vastly outweighs write traffic (new tweets).

fields.Front: Write the REST endpoint to post a new tweet.
Write the REST endpoint to fetch a user's home timeline.
Write a minimal schema for the tweets table.
fields.Back:
tweets(
  tweet_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id    BIGINT,
  text       VARCHAR(280),
  media_urls TEXT[],
  created_at TIMESTAMP
)

fields.Front: Write a minimal schema for the follows table modeling the social graph.
fields.Back:
follows(
  follower_id BIGINT,
  followee_id BIGINT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
)

fields.Front: Why is it useful to also index follows by followee_id (a reverse index)?
fields.Back: The fanout-on-write process needs to quickly find all followers of a user who just tweeted, which requires querying by followee_id — a forward-only index on follower_id can't serve that efficiently.

fields.Front: Why is a message queue placed between tweet creation and the fanout service?
fields.Back: It decouples ingestion from fanout so tweet writes return quickly, and lets the fanout service process work asynchronously and absorb bursts without blocking writers.

fields.Front: What is the main tradeoff between fanout-on-write and fanout-on-read?
fields.Back: Fanout-on-write makes reads fast but writes expensive (and wastes work fanning out to inactive followers); fanout-on-read makes writes cheap but reads slow/expensive, especially for users who follow many people.

fields.Front: What is the 'celebrity problem' in feed fanout design?
fields.Back: A user with millions of followers (e.g. a celebrity) triggers fanout-on-write to millions of inboxes per tweet, creating a massive write spike and hot-key pressure that can overwhelm the fanout system.

fields.Front: What is the standard hybrid solution to the celebrity problem?
fields.Back: Use fanout-on-write for regular users, but fanout-on-read (pull) for celebrities/high-follower accounts — at read time, merge the follower's precomputed timeline with a live query of tweets from any celebrities they follow.

fields.Front: How does caching precomputed timelines in Redis help scale feed reads?
fields.Back: It avoids recomputing/merging tweets from all followees on every read, serving most timeline requests directly from an in-memory cache, cutting database load and latency dramatically.

fields.Front: Why does a Twitter-like system accept eventual consistency for the timeline instead of strong consistency?
fields.Back: Strong consistency across a globally distributed, fanned-out feed system would add significant write latency and reduce availability; a few seconds of delay before a tweet appears in followers' feeds is an acceptable UX tradeoff for much higher throughput and availability.
When a user tweets, the tweet is immediately pushed into the precomputed timeline/inbox of every follower, so reads are fast (just fetch the precomputed list).
A user's timeline is assembled at read time by querying and merging tweets from everyone they follow, so writes are cheap but reads are more expensive.
